title: TA7-08846
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXXX XXXXXX XXXXXX XXXXXX (the principal claimant hereinafter called "the claimant"), his wife XXXXX XXXXXX XXXXXX XXXXX (hereinafter call the "wife") and their children, all minor claimants, XXXXXX XXXXXX XXXXXX, XXXXXX XXXXXX XXXXXX, XXXXXX XXXXXX XXXXXX and XXXXXX XXXXXX XXXXXX seek refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 Designated Representative

The principal claimant XXXXX XXXXXX XXXXXX XXXXX was designated as the representative for the four minor claimants named above. At the hearing, the claimant confirmed his agreement to act as his children's designated representative.
The claimant alleges the following.
He was born in XXXX, Nigeria on XXXX, 1964. He is married and has four children. He is a member of the Igbo tribe.

The claimant joined the Movement for the Actualization of the Sovereign State of Biafra (MASSOB) in 2004 in order to help bring development into his region. In XXXX 2005, the claimant withdrew from the MASSOB organization because he disagreed with violent methods that were being used by some members.

On XXXX, 2007, the claimant's farm home was surrounded by members of MASSOB. The claimant escaped but his home was destroyed in a fire set by these men. He reported the incident to the police. The police identified the claimant as a member of MASSOB; they detained him for a few hours. He gained his release through bribery.

On XXXX, 2007, the claimant's younger brother XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX was killed. One XXXX, 2007, the manager of the claimant's XXXX XXXX was shot and killed. Graffiti was left on the wall of the shop naming the claimant as the target of the assault. On XXXX, 2007 a group of men attended the claimant's home in XXXX looking for him. He was not at home. The claimant's wife was beaten and raped. His children were hit and locked in one room of their home. The claimant believes that members of MASSOB were looking for him in each of these incidents.
The claimant's wife makes the same allegations as the claimant.
The four minor children depend upon the allegations of the claimant and his wife.
The claimant, his wife and children left Nigeria on XXXX, 2007. They arrived in Canada on XXXX, 2007 and made their claims for refugee protection on the following day.

The panel finds that XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXX and their children, XXXXXXXXXXXXXX, XXXXXXXXXXXXXX, XXXX XXXXXXXXXX and XXXXXXXXXXXXXX, are not Convention refugees pursuant to s. 96 of the IRPA, nor are they persons in need of protection, pursuant to s. 97 of IRPA.
The issues in this hearing were: * Political identity, * Credibility. The Hearing
The hearing began in the afternoon of June 17, 2010 and at approximately 5 p.m. the hearing was adjourned. The hearing reconvened on October 19, 2010. Identity

The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, the claimant, his wife and four minor children are who they say they are and that they are citizens of Nigeria. In support of their identities, the claimant, his wife and four minor children each provided a copy of their Nigerian passports.2 Credibility

After careful consideration of all of the evidence and representations, the panel finds that there is insufficient credible and trustworthy evidence with regard to pivotal areas of the claimant's oral and written evidence. The claimant has failed to advance his claim with evidence that is consistent or credible. The panel is aware that none of the credibility concerns raised here may be sufficient, each on its own, to negate this claim. However, the cumulative effect of all of them is that the panel does not have sufficient credible and trustworthy evidence upon which to base a determination that the claimant is a Convention refugee. As the Federal Court of Appeal in Sheikh,3 MacGuigan, J.A. held: even without disbelieving every word [a claimant] has uttered, a ... panel may reasonably find him so lacking in credibility that it concludes that there is no credible evidence relevant to his claim ... In other words, a general finding of a lack of credibility on the part of the applicant may concurrently extend to all relevant information emanating from his testimony.

The panel is not persuaded that the claimant was a member of MASSOB. His testimony was not reasonable in terms of the claimant's alleged role within MASSOB and the relationship between the MASSOB and the Nigerian government. In his Personal Information Form (PIF) narrative4 and during his testimony, the claimant explained that as a successful Igbo businessman he was a XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. He stated that he would XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXX and XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. He testified that he joined MASSOB because it occurred to him that his people, the Igbo, had fought in a civil war and that Nigeria did not care about the Igbo's welfare. The claimant stated that as a member of MASSOB he would attend large meetings. He explained that members were sent notices to advise them of the MASSOB meetings. The claimant testified that he was a respected businessman and he convinced others to joined MASSSOB by explaining that individual people cannot approach the government with their concerns but they could use MASSOB as a bridge to the government. The claimant testified that when he joined MASSOB in 2004 it was a peaceful organization. The panel is not persuaded that the claimant's activities with MASSOB are credible. The panel finds it not credible that the MASSOB sent out notices to members to inform them of meetings. Documentary evidence indicates that anyone possessing leaflets or other similar objects from the MASSOB could be arrested and charged with treason, an offence punishable by death.5 It is not reasonable that the organization would use printed announcements that would put its members at such risk. The claimant provided no persuasive evidence that the government accepts representations from MASSOB for the interests of the Igbo people. It is not credible that the claimant would XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX and in turn MASSOB would XXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. The panel prefers the independent documents before it which indicate that MASSOB has been banned by the Nigerian government since 2001 or 2002 and that the former president of Nigeria, Olusegan Obasanjo, stated that MASSOB should be destroyed. The documents indicate that the Nigerian government takes action against organizations, such as MASSOB, that threaten the unity of the country.6 The MASSOB is seen as a clear threat by the political elite who wish to secure their own position.7 The panel infers from these documents that the federal government would not accept concerns from MASSOB regarding the Igbo people as the claimant has alleged. The panel pointed out these independent documents to the claimant and asked him to explain the contradiction. The claimant's description of MASSOB's activities and explanation to the contradictions were incoherent and lacked detail. He testified that MASSOB was begun by ex-Biafran soldiers who were not bad but wanted to create a bridge with the government. He said when agitation began in the organization, the government stated that MASSOB was not a good organization. He testified that MASSOB members recruited people in eastern Nigeria to become conduits to the government. He testified that the documents were right and the government had no choice but to ban MASSOB when some troublesome people became violent. The panel finds that the claimant did not explain the contradiction with his answer. His answer indicates a lack of understanding of the MASSOB organization as described in the country documents. The independent documents state that MASSOB began in 1999 as a separatist group espousing Igbo unity and the secession of the Igbo-majority states8 not as a bridge to the Nigerian government as the claimant alleges. The Response to Information Request NGA103196.FE9 states that between May 2000 and April 2008 "over 2,000 of its [MASSOB] members were killed by Nigerian security forces ... and over 1,000 [are] languishing in various prisons in the country." The panel questioned the claimant about the contradiction between his statement that MASSOB was a peaceful organization when he joined and the documentary evidence regarding the organization's history of involvement in violent behaviour with government forces. He stated that MASSOB was peaceful when he joined in XXXX 2004 but youth in the organization began to deviate. He said that when people began to be killed he decided to leave MASSOB and he resigned in XXXX 2005. The claimant's explanation is not satisfactory as it did not explain the contradiction and actually contradicted the documentary evidence again. The panel believes the claimant has presented this unreasonable scenario as a way to explain why he, as an educated businessman, would have joined MASSOB. The panel believes the claimant has fabricated his membership in MASSOB and the consequences of that association in order to make a claim for refugee protection.

The panel finds contradictions within the claimant's Port of Entry notes10 and between these notes and his PIF narrative regarding his membership in and fear of MASSOB. The claimant was detained and had more than one interview at the Port of Entry. During an interview on XXXX, 2007 at the Port of Entry, the claimant stated he was a member of MASSOB XXXX from XXXX 2002 to XXXX 2007 whereas the claimant testified that he joined MASSOB in XXXX, 2004 and resigned in XXXX, 2005. In the XXXX, 2007 Port of Entry interview, the claimant stated that he was afraid the government might kill him but that he did not know why this was so. He stated that the government is "getting the number of the MASSOB." During a Port of Entry interview two days later, on XXXX, 2007, the claimant stated that he feared persecution by the government because where he lives there is oil and a lot of fighting and killings. The panel notes that the claimant did not state any fear of the MASSOB during either POE interview. The officer at the second, XXXX, 2007, interview noted that this was a different claim than noted on the earlier file. The claim made at the first POE interview implied fear of the government and some connection with MASSOB while the second claim implied fear of the government due to fighting over oil. The panel notes that the country documents nowhere mention that MASSOB is an organization associated with the fighting over the oil resources in Nigeria.11 In his PIF narrative and during his testimony, the claimant stated that MASSOB members tried to kill him and that others were killed by MASSOB because of their association with him. The claimant was asked to explain the discrepancies between the POE and the PIF narrative/ testimony. He testified that his agent who arranged for him to travel to Canada had advised him to first speak to a lawyer upon arrival in Canada. He testified that a lawyer met with him at the airport and told him what to say. He explained that the lawyer wrote down the claimant's recollections and read the report to him, that he did not know what was obtained during the interview, and that he had eventually dispensed with this lawyer. The panel does not find the claimant's explanations satisfactory. The panel reasonably believes that a lawyer assisting the claimant would record the information the claimant gave him; not tell him what to say. It is the claimant, not the lawyer, who is responsible for the information in the POE notes and whether the claimant had a lawyer or not would not prevent the claimant from knowing what he feared. The claimant's apparent attempt to blame the lawyer does not satisfactorily explain the discrepancies. The claimant was asked specifically about not mentioning fearing MASSOB during either of his interviews at the POE. The claimant explained that he had stated MASSOB at the Port of Entry interviews and then he testified that he was unable to remember what he said. The panel does not find the claimant's explanation reasonable. He did list membership in the MASSOB. However, in neither Port of Entry interview does the claimant state that he feared MASSOB. His alleged association with and then threats by MASSOB are pivotal to his claim. It is not reasonable that he would have mentioned nothing of his fear of MASSOB at the Port of Entry, only his membership. The claimant fled Nigeria not long before his interview at the POE. He testified that he fled for one reason, that he feared persecution from MASSOB members. It is not reasonable that under these particular circumstances, unique to the claimant, within less than a week of his flight from Nigeria he would provide some other reason for his fear of persecution.

The claimant testified that a number of people closely associated with him were seriously harmed by members of MASSOB because of their relationship with him. The claimant testified that members of MASSOB attacked his farm and forced him to run for his life. The claimant testified that his brother XXXX and his manager XXXX XXXX were murdered by members of MASSOB. The claimant testified that his family home in Lagos was attacked, his wife raped, and children threatened when members of MASSOB were looking for him. The claimant was asked how he knew that the people who attacked his farm, his manager, his brother and his wife and children were members of MASSOB. He testified that it was just his suspicion. The panel finds that the claimant's allegations that members of MASSOB are responsible for these various attacks are mere speculation. The panel will now discuss the lack of credibility of the claimant's testimony regarding some of these attacks.

The panel is not persuaded that the claimant's brother, XXXX XXXX XXXX, was killed by members of MASSOB. In the claimant's amended PIF narrative, the claimant states that XXXX was stabbed to death. During the first hearing on June 17, 2010, the claimant testified that XXXX was killed on XXXX, 2007 when members of MASSOB were looking for the claimant. He provided as evidence a copy of the death certificate of XXXX XXXX XXXX which states the date of death as XXXX, 2007 and "death by unknown persons."12 The claimant provided a copy of a statement13 he sent to Amnesty International (AI) on XXXX, 2008, after he had arrived in Canada, in which he states that his brother, XXXX XXXX XXXX, was killed by four gunmen on XXXX, 2008 during the kidnapping of his mother. This date of death is almost two years after the other date of death of the same brother XXXX. In the statement to AI he also states that he suspects his step-brother XXXX of having XXXX killed because of financial troubles between XXXX and XXXX. At the first hearing, the claimant was asked to explain the discrepancies in the nature and date of his brother XXXX death. The claimant testified that what he wrote to AI was not correct. He explained that he was in a delirious state of mind because of his mother's kidnapping. The claimant testified that he was on medication at the time he wrote to AI and that his memory is not good. The panel does not find the claimant's explanation reasonable. While the alleged kidnapping of his mother might make the claimant extremely upset, it is not reasonable that he would provide a completely different scenario of his brother's death than he did in his amended PIF narrative and testimony. The panel does not accept loss of memory as a reasonable explanation for the discrepancies. Indeed, fabricating a story is not an issue of memory loss. Regardless, the panel observed during the first hearing that the claimant did not present any significant memory difficulties. An important indicator of credibility is whether a witness can consistently tell his particular story.14 The panel believes that the claimant is not credible because he was not consistent with the story regarding XXXX alleged death at the hands of MASSOB members because of XXXX relationship with the claimant. The panel will further address the claimant's medical reason for the contradictions in the next paragraph.

At the beginning of the resumption of the hearing on October 19, 2010 the claimant provided a medical document from his family physician dated October 18, 2010 and a copy of letter from his counsel to the physician, dated June 21, 2010. Counsel's letter requests a report on the claimant's "medical/psychological condition."15 The panel waived the twenty day rule for submission of these two documents. The panel notes that a medical report was not requested from the claimant's physician until the discrepancy regarding the claimant's brother's death had been flagged at the earlier hearing. The panel believes if the claimant had a medical condition that impaired his memory that a medical report would have been provided before the commencement of the first hearing. The claimant was asked why the medical documentation was not provided earlier. He explained that he was not able to make the request until recently and that he made the request in June, 2010. Counsel submitted that he sent a request to the claimant's doctor immediately after the first hearing. The panel does not find that the claimant's explanation reasonable. The claimant did not explain why he could not make an earlier request and, indeed, the panel believes a request could have been made any time in the past two years. The counsel's submission did not remove the panel's concern that the medical evidence was requested only after a serious discrepancy had been pointed out to the claimant during the first hearing. Nevertheless, the doctor diagnosed the claimant as having Post Traumatic Stress Disorder and Major Depression. The letter states that the psychiatry service at the doctor's hospital confirmed this diagnosis. The panel accepts the diagnosis. The doctor states that the claimant is currently being treated with antidepressants and is awaiting assessment for "so-called organic brain dysfunction." The letter does not state when the claimant was diagnosed or when he began using antidepressants. Nowhere does the letter state that the claimant's memory is affected by his medical conditions or the prescribed medication. The doctor states that the claimant's condition "is entirely consistent with the story he tells me and there is no doubt that the events he suffered through caused his current condition." The doctor also referred to the "repeated head trauma" that the claimant suffered; this is information that the claimant did not himself present for his claim. The doctor is not in a position to know that the allegations made by the claimant occurred. The doctor's diagnosis may or may not be related to the causes described by the claimant in his evidence. The panel refers to Danailov, with respect to the assessment of a physician's evidence and the question of the assessment of credibility, in which it was stated "that opinion evidence is only as valid as the truth of the facts on which it is based."16 Also relevant to the doctor's opinion is the position in Rokni; a psychiatric report submitted as evidence "cannot possibly serve as a cure-all for any and all deficiencies in a claimant's testimony."17 The panel gives little weight to the medical evidence and does not accept the claimant's alleged memory problems for the discrepancies regarding his brother's death.

The panel is not persuaded that the claimant's wife and children were attacked by members of MASSOB in XXXX in XXXX 2007. As stated earlier, an important indicator of credibility is whether a witness can consistently tell his particular story.18 The panel found that there were contradictions in the claimant's amended PIF narrative and his testimony regarding the alleged attack on his family in their XXXX home. The claimant testified that he was out visiting friends when a neighbour called him to say that he had heard gunshots from the claimant's home. The claimant was asked why he did not mention in his amended PIF narrative the use of guns when his family was attacked. The claimant explained that he was sure he wrote this in his PIF and then he testified that he had some relation who was hit by the butt of a gun. The panel does not accept the claimant's explanation. The claimant's explanation expresses his uncertainty and the panel believes that the claimant would remember something as serious as his family being threatened by a gun and thus would have included it in his amended PIF. In his original PIF narrative, the claimant stated that his brothers were hit with "gun heads" in an incident at the claimant's farm home sometime before the alleged attack at his XXXX home. The claimant was not able to keep his story straight and the panel finds the claimant's contradictions further undermines his credibility. The claimant continued to give testimony regarding the attack on his family and stated that his wife was unconscious when he arrived home. The claimant was asked why his wife's unconscious state was not mentioned in his PIF narrative or in the medical report19 he provided. The claimant testified that his wife gave him details of what happened to her when she gained consciousness in the hospital. However, the panel finds that the claimant's answer did not satisfactorily explain why he did not mention his wife's unconscious state in his PIF narrative or why it was not mentioned in the medical report. The claimant testified that his wife was raped by the attackers. He was asked why he did not state this serious allegation in his PIF. The panel finds that the claimant did not give a satisfactory explanation when he testified that he was sure that he wrote it in his PIF. Counsel submitted that for the claimant to report his wife's rape would be hearsay. The panel does not accept counsel's submission as satisfactorily explaining why the claimant would not state a critical aspect of the claim. Many of the incidents reported by the claimant are hearsay, such as the alleged attack on his family's home, the alleged murders of his brother and manager and the alleged kidnapping of the claimant's mother. The claimant's testimony with regard to the alleged attack on his home by MASSOB members further compromises his credibility.

The claimant's wife testified that she did not remember anything concerned with arriving at the hospital after the attack on their home. When the wife was asked if she was raped she was quiet for some time, then stated that she was being emotional, and eventually testified that she was raped. The sworn testimony of a claimant is presumed to be truthful unless there is valid reason to doubt its truthfulness.20 The panel kept Chairperson's Guideline 421 in mind when considering the wife's testimony. The panel has concern regarding the medical evidence provided by the claimant regarding the alleged rape of his wife; the panel will address this concern in the following paragraph. Nevertheless, the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the wife was raped. As distressing and unfortunate as the rape may be, the panel is not persuaded, for a number of reasons, that members of MASSOB are responsible for the rape. In the first instance, the panel refers to the previous paragraph and repeats that it is not persuaded that the claimant's home and family were attacked by members of MASSOB. Secondly, the independent documentary evidence and documentary evidence provided by the claimant 22 does not support the claimant's allegations of MASSOB being an organization that initiates violence against its own members which the claimant alleges. The documentary evidence indicates that the MASSOB was founded on the philosophy of non-violence and that their activities include education of the Igbo people and peaceful demonstrations against the Nigerian government. The violence that the MASSOB members have been involved in has been against government forces as a result of the actions of the government taken against them. The panel believes that the rape was a random act of violence.

The panel has concerns regarding the medical evidence provided to support the allegation that the wife was raped by members of MASSOB. The claimant testified that his wife was given medical attention at a private clinic. The claimant provided a letter from XXXX Hospital written by Dr. XXXX.23 The letter is evidence that the claimant's wife suffered a lacerated thumb and was raped. The panel finds the letter problematic. The letter does not state that she was unconscious as the claimant testified and his wife implied during her testimony. The two page medical report states that she was examined and noted to have "Semen ++ within the vagina" and "Emotional brakedown [sic] as rape and its discussion is like a taboo and usually better not discussed." However, other than these two sentences regarding rape, the two page report focuses on the damage to and follow-up treatment to the wife's thumb. The panel does not find reasonable the lack of attention by medical staff to an alleged rape and emotional breakdown with the conclusion "better not discussed." The independent documentary evidence does not support such lack of medical intervention for a rape and emotional breakdown. The independent documentary evidence24 indicates that private hospitals provide a higher standard of care than public sector hospitals and some meet United States' standards. The same documentary evidence indicates that psychiatric care is available as are various therapeutic drugs. The industry of fraudulent documents in Nigeria25 and the questionable information in the report as well as the claimant's contradictory information [stating his wife was unconscious which the medical evidence does not state] leads the panel to find this alleged medical document to be unreliable and, on a balance of probabilities, fraudulently obtained.

The panel is not persuaded that two people have been killed and one kidnapped by MASSOB agents because of their association with the claimant. The panel believes that the claimant embellished his claim with these allegations. The panel has previously discussed the claimant's lack of credible testimony regarding the alleged death of his brother XXXX XXXX XXXX at the hands of MASSOB members. The claimant testified and stated in his PIF narrative that his mother was kidnapped in 2008 by MASSOB members looking for him. In his letter to AI, the claimant stated that he suspected his step-brother was responsible for the kidnapping and gave the reason as financial difficulties within the family. The claimant was asked to explain the contradictions between his PIF narrative/testimony and the letter to AI regarding those responsible for kidnapping his mother. The claimant testified that sometime after the kidnapping someone called him in Canada and told him that it was a secret that MASSOB was behind his mother's kidnapping. The panel does not find the claimant's explanation satisfactory and believes he embellished his claim with this allegation. The claimant provided copies of letters from his sister XXXX as evidence of his mother's kidnapping.26 In a letter dated XXXX, 200727 (written a year before the alleged kidnapping) XXXX states that the "village chief ...is trying to figure out what is going on while innocent men and their family members die." She also states that she is aware that the claimant is concerned about his farm and factory in Nigeria. In her letter dated XXXX, 2008, written shortly after the kidnapping, XXXX states that it is "criminals that kidnapped our mom for ransom had been negotiating with our relatives" and "they [the criminals] want to talk to you [the claimant]." She also states that the family has "heard of government officials, businessmen, politicians' kids and wifes [sic] kidnapped for ransom and or killed."28 In XXXX letter written XXXX, 200929 she tells the claimant that a neighbour in Nigeria was kidnapped "this month." In a letter30 dated XXXX, 2008, a family member, XXXX XXXX, in Nigeria, states that the claimant's mother was kidnapped by "unknown people." XXXX letters and XXXX letter provide no persuasive evidence that those responsible for kidnapping his mother are members of MASSOB wanting to kill the claimant. The panel infers from the letters that criminals in the claimant's home area are using kidnapping as a method of gaining money. The claimant testified that members of MASSOB killed his manager XXXX XXXX and left graffiti on the wall stating that the claimant was the actual target of the shooting. The claimant provided an affidavit from XXXX XXXX, XXXX brother, as evidence of this allegation.31 The affidavit states that XXXX XXXX was killed while working at the XXXX owned by the claimant. The affidavit neither refers to threatening graffiti left on the wall nor states the cause of XXXX death. Other than his own testimony, the panel finds the claimant has provided no persuasive evidence that XXXX XXXX death was a result of the claimant's alleged involvement with MASSOB. The panel reasonably assumes that XXXX XXXX would, at the very least, state the cause of his brother's death given that the affidavit was provided for the claimant's case. The panel also refers its earlier finding that the claimant is speculating when he alleges that XXXX XXXX was killed by MASSOB members.

The claimant's wife had a separate PIF narrative and amended narrative which repeats her husband's allegations regarding the MASSOB. As stated above, that while panel accepts, on a balance of probabilities, that the wife was raped, the panel is not persuaded that the rape was perpetrated by members of MASSOB looking for the claimant.

After considering all of the evidence, the panel concludes that the claimant is not credible and has, therefore, not satisfied the burden of establishing a serious possibility that he would be persecuted for a Convention ground. As the panel stated at the outset, it is aware that none of the credibility concerns raised here may be sufficient, each on its own, to negate this claim. However, given that these concerns touch upon such important, central issues in the claim, the cumulative effect is that the panel does not have sufficient credible and trustworthy evidence upon which to base a determination that the claimant is a Convention refugee. Since the wife made the same allegations as her husband, the panel concludes that she has not satisfied the burden of establishing a serious possibility that she will be persecuted on Convention grounds. Since the four minor claimants are dependent upon the claimant's and the wife's allegations, the panel concludes they have not satisfied the burden of establishing a serious possibility that they would be persecuted on Convention grounds. Section 97(1)
The claimant advanced no evidence to suggest he would face any danger, that is more likely than not, of torture within the meaning of Article 1 of the "Convention Against Torture."

Given the panel's finding, that the claimant is not a credible witness, the panel finds that he is not a person who faces a serious risk to his life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if he were to return to Nigeria. For the same reason the panel finds that the wife and four minor claimants are not persons who face a serious risk to their lives or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if they were to return to Nigeria.

The panel determines that the claimants are not Convention refugees and not persons in need of protection in accordance with section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the IRPA. Accordingly, after consideration of the totality of the evidence, the panel rejects the claims. (signed) "L. Mason" L.
